name: Koalib-Rere
sweep_summary: Koalib-Rere (koal1240, Heibanic) is not in the catalog. The one sweep item, Chai, Kunda, Rodríguez & Rose 2022 'Prosody of declaratives and questions in Rere (Koalib)' (OUP, DOI 10.1093/oso/9780198869740.003.0011), is a sentence-intonation study of a tone language (boundary tones L%/H%, H lowering, upsweep, clitic tones per the Crossref abstract and Google Books snippets pp. 298-331); it is paywalled (OUP 403, Unpaywall closed, no author PDF), and nothing reachable from it mentions word stress. Extra open sources fetched sources and read with): Quint 2006 'Do you speak Kordofanian?' (§II.4: 'Koalib is a tone language... two tone levels' plus falling tone), Quint 2024 imperatives (§2.1: two phonological tones H/L, contour F=HL, citing Quint 2006: 145-165; 2009: 129-148), Quint & Koko 2025, Quint 2022 (acute in Koalib marks tone, whereas in non-tonal Nyun it marks 'accent tonique'), Boychev 2013 MA thesis, and the open-access Demir Nalci, Kunda & Rose 2025 SAL paper (§2.1: 'Rere has two level tones, H, L, and a falling HL'). None contains any statement on word stress or accent placement. No best new stress statement found. Highest-priority unread source: Quint (& Kokko) 2009 The Phonology of Koalib, Rüdiger Köppe (chapters on vowels, consonants, tonal system, syllable structure, orthography; HAL record halshs-00584041 without file; publisher PDF for sale; Harvard print WID PL8393.95.N57 Q5613 2009), plus its 2006 French original (L'Harmattan; Harvard print PL8393). Google Books search-within for 'stress'/'accent' inside the OUP volume was rate-limited, so a remark on word-level prominence inside the Chai et al. chapter cannot be excluded (medium priority).

sources.citation: Demir Nalci, Nese, Titus Kubri Kajo Kunda & Sharon Rose. 2025 [issue dated 2024]. Tone patterns in Rere (Koalib) inalienable possessives. Studies in African Linguistics 53(1&2): 1-24.
sources.quote: Rere has two level tones, H, L, and a falling HL (Quint 2009). (1) a. ŋwɔ́ɲ H ‘saliva’ / ŋwɔ̀ɲ L ‘eggs’ b. ŋáò HL ‘water’ / ŋàò L ‘femininity, womanhood, beauty’
sources.note: Describes the lexical tone system only (two level tones plus falling HL; tone expones case); the words 'stress', 'accent' and 'prominence' do not occur anywhere in the 24 pages. Silent on word stress.

sources.citation: Quint, Nicolas. 2024. Koalib imperatives and semantically related forms (40 pp.); Quint & Koko. 2025. Verb extensions in Koalib (45 pp.); Quint. 2022. Classes nominales... le koalib. Faits de Langues 52(2) (27 pp.); Boychev, Georgi. 2013. Case inflection in Koalib: discovering the rules. MA thesis, Université de Lorraine (50 pp.).
sources.quote: Koalib has two phonological tones (Quint 2006: 145–165; 2009: 129–148), namely high (H, see (1)), and low (L, see (2)). It also has several contour tones, the most frequent being a falling tone (F, see (3)), which can ultimately be analyzed as a succession of a high and a low tone, i.e., F=HL. [Quint 2024] — En koalib, les accents représentent les tons (haut (aigu) [á], bas (grave) [à], modulé descendant ... [Quint 2022: 'In Koalib the accent marks represent tones (high (acute), low (grave), falling ...)']
sources.locator: Quint 2024 §2.1 (p. 2); Quint 2022 fn. on transcription (p. 4 of PDF, line 210 of text dump); Boychev 2013 §1 pp. 4-5
sources.note: All four are morphosyntactic works whose phonological preliminaries describe only the H/L(+HL) tone system and vowel harmony; the only occurrences of 'stress' (Quint 2024, 2 hits) are the ordinary verb 'to stress a point'. Quint 2022 contrasts Koalib (acute = high tone) with Nyun, 'langue non tonale', where the acute marks 'la place de l'accent tonique' — a stress statement for Nyun, not for Koalib. Silent on Koalib word stress.

sources.citation: Quint, Nicolas. 2006. Do you speak Kordofanian? Paper presented at the 7th International Sudan Studies Conference, University of Bergen, 6-8 April 2006. 16 pp.
sources.quote: Like most of Niger-Congo languages (Clements 2000 : 152 ; Creissels 1994 : 177), Koalib is a tone language, i.e. the tonal melody associated to each syllable of a word has a distinctive value. Koalib has two tone levels : - high, signaled by an acute accent [...] : ŋwóny saliva. - low, signaled by a grave accent [...] : ŋwòny eggs. These two levels can combine to form several types of modulations, the most common of which is the falling tone (begins high and ends low), signaled by a circumflex accent : ŋâo water.
sources.note: First-hand sketch by the language's principal describer: Koalib is a two-level tone language with lexical and heavy grammatical tone (case and person marked by tone alone). No mention of stress or word-level prominence anywhere in the paper.

sources.access_detail: only an abstract or snippet reachable
sources.quote: The prosodic system of declarative sentences and questions in Rere (Koalib), a Niger-Congo language of Sudan, is characterized by pitch raising and lowering, which target boundary positions and particular tones. Declarative utterances are marked by a final L% boundary tone. [...] Polar questions are marked by a final low-toned clitic. [...] Finally, a high tone added at the left edge of the verb marks wh-ex-situ questions as well as similar constructions.
sources.locator: Crossref abstract; Google Books search-within snippets pp. 298, 303, 309, 315, 323, 329, 331
sources.note: The abstract and every reachable snippet treat sentence-level intonation (boundary tones L%/H%, H-tone lowering, upsweep, clitic tones) in a language whose words carry lexical H/L tone; nothing reachable mentions word stress or accent placement. The chapter is paywalled at OUP (403 on landing and chapter PDF; Unpaywall: closed; not on Rose's publications page as a PDF; Google Books search-within for 'stress'/'accent' was rate-limited, only the 'Koalib' query returned snippets).
